source: Frischkorn and Oberauer (2021) Intelligence test items varying in capacity demands cannot be used to test the causality of working memory capacity for fluid intelligence, Psychon Bull Rev 28, 1423-1432
finding: Simulation of three capacity models (Generic, Slot, Resource). Under the capacity hypothesis itself, the item-wise WMC correlation can rise, fall or stay flat with demand. The test used by Little et al. and Dokic et al. is therefore not diagnostic.
numbers: Simulated N = 100, 250, 500; 17 Raven-type items with 1-4 rule tokens; 1,000 runs per cell, 12,000 per model. Correlation peaks where sample mean WMC equals item demand (mean WMC minus rule tokens = 0).
quote: The capacity hypothesis does not imply stronger correlations of WMC and intelligence test items with higher capacity demands.
limits: Simulation only; depends on the assumed response models. Pattern also scales with the strength of the WMC-theta link.
agent_relevance: Do not read a flat rule-count curve as proof that capacity does not matter. Use direct experimental manipulation of one process.

source: Frischkorn and Oberauer (2021) Intelligence test items varying in capacity demands cannot be used to test the causality of working memory capacity for fluid intelligence, Psychon Bull Rev 28, 1423-1432 (model details)
finding: Generic and Slot models: in low-WMC samples correlations fall as demand rises; in high-WMC samples they rise. Resource model: mostly falling, near quadratic in high-WMC samples; the highest-demand items never beat medium-demand items.
numbers: Mean Pearson r .33-.41 vs point-biserial .23-.29; ordinal pattern agreement .91-.98.
limits: Authors say Little et al. (2014) was the only prior study with increasing correlations; they replicated the Smolen quadratic pattern but saw decreases for easy items before floor.
agent_relevance: The right difficulty variable is demand relative to the solver capacity. An agent effective capacity should be measured per model before predicting where rule count bites.

source: Smolen and Chuderski (2015) The quadratic relationship between difficulty of intelligence test items and their correlations with working memory, Frontiers in Psychology 6:1270
finding: Raven APM item-wise WMC correlation is an inverted U over difficulty, not linear. Linear fit was null; quadratic and segmented fits were clearly better.
numbers: Sample 1 N = 347 (complex span, r with Raven .51); Sample 2 N = 939 (r .43). Linear F(1,34)=0.4 p=.53; segmented adj R2 .17 (breakpoint error .44; r .46 below, -.52 above); N=939 segmented adj R2 .22 (breakpoint .42; r .53 below, -.50 above). 9-bin model fit RMSD .028 and .026.
limits: Authors argue floor and ceiling effects, not storage vs attention, create the shape; so the test cannot discriminate theories.
agent_relevance: Item-level correlation is contaminated by floor and ceiling. Expect the same artefact in LLM item analyses with near-0% or near-100% items.

source: Smolen and Chuderski (2015), floor and ceiling simulations
finding: Simulations show how much floor or ceiling cuts an item correlation, so extreme items always show weak links.
numbers: 100,000 observations per sample; base r .5 fell to .45 with about 25% on floor and stayed above .25 until floor shift 2.61; analytically, half of scores at floor/ceiling cuts r from 1.0 to .86.
limits: Assumes a simple threshold model.
agent_relevance: Drop or down-weight items with accuracy near chance or near 100% before drawing conclusions about demand.

source: Smolen and Chuderski (2015), new-rule vs old-rule recoding
finding: Wiley et al. (2011) claim that new-rule items drive the link was not supported on re-coding.
numbers: 18 new-rule vs 18 old-rule items, N = 347: mean r .223 vs .197, z(34)=1.41, p=.17.
limits: Single sample; coding taken from Wiley.
agent_relevance: Novelty of rule combination is not a reliable difficulty axis either.

source: Little, Lewandowsky and Craig (2014) Working memory capacity and fluid abilities: the more difficult the item, the more more is better, Front Psychol 5:239
finding: Only positive result: WMC composite correlates more with later (harder) Raven items, but only when the overall WMC-Raven correlation is moderate to high. Earlier nulls explained as low overall correlation.
numbers: N = 126 analysed (130 recruited), 4 WM tasks composite, RAPM Set II 36 items. Composite WMC r with RAPM = .56; item-wise slope .004, t(34)=2.87, p<.01, r2=.20. OSPAN alone r=.36, slope n.s. (t(34)=1.39). Simulation: slope .0002 at rho .1 up to .0016 at rho .9.
limits: Item order used as difficulty proxy; small, mostly female student sample; slope reported .004 in text and .005 in figure caption; novelty effect not significant (p=.39).
agent_relevance: The supportive evidence rests on a composite WM score and item position, both weak proxies. Treat as a minority finding.

source: Little et al. (2014), rule-token multilevel model
finding: More rule tokens lower accuracy, and high-WMC people lose less from extra tokens (small interaction).
numbers: Tokens beta = -0.10 (SE .005), p<.001; zWMC x tokens beta = .02 (SE .007), p<.01; zWMC x item position .001 (SE .0005), p<.01. Wiley (2011) token-wise r = .25, .24, .33, .21 for 1-4 tokens.
limits: Several items excluded for technical reasons; interaction tiny; token-wise r from Wiley show no rise.
agent_relevance: Rule tokens do lower accuracy, so they are a real difficulty input, but the capacity-specific part is small.

source: Chuderski (2013) When are fluid intelligence and working memory isomorphic and when are they not? Intelligence 41, 244-262
finding: Time pressure is a strong moderator of the WM-Gf link. With half the usual time, WM and Gf were statistically indistinguishable; with near-unlimited time WM explained only 38% of Gf variance.
numbers: Study 1 N = 890 (298 speeded, 289 moderate, 303 unspeeded). Latent r = 1.0 speeded, .83 moderate, .62 unspeeded (differences p=.017 and p=.004). Observed corrected r .65 vs .46, p<.001.
limits: Study 1 partly reanalysed old datasets; WM tasks few. Interpretation (relational learning during test) is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: If the capacity bottleneck depends on time, the agent compute or token budget per step may play the role of time. Slower, deliberate runs may escape the limit.

source: Chuderski (2013), literature review of 26 studies
finding: Across 26 Raven-WM studies the mean WM-Raven correlation falls as allowed time rises.
numbers: Highly speeded (<=30 min): 55 correlations, N = 2253, mean r .395. Moderate (40 min): 41 correlations, N = 1847, r .316. Unspeeded (>=45 min): 11 correlations, N = 553, r .263.
limits: Between-study comparison, confounded by sample, WM task and country; unspeeded set is small.
agent_relevance: Large part of the mixed literature on the capacity link may be a time-limit artefact, a third axis beside item difficulty and rule count.

source: Chuderski (2013), item accuracy by time
finding: Time pressure hurt late (hard) items far more than early ones.
numbers: Accuracy loss in the first half of the tests small (about 3.7%) vs 17.6% in the second half when time was cut.
limits: Percentages as read from the text; test sets Raven plus an analogy test.
agent_relevance: Hard items are mostly not attempted under pressure, so hard-item correlations under speed reflect omissions, not capacity.

source: Chuderski (2015) The broad factor of working memory is virtually isomorphic to fluid intelligence tested under time pressure, Pers Individ Differ 85, 98-104
finding: Replicated the time effect with a better WM battery (four WM functions: storage, attention control, relational integration, updating).
numbers: N = 264 timed; broad WM factor shared 83.4% variance with timed Gf; reanalysis of untimed data gave 58.2%. In timed tests only the easy early items contributed to the WM-Gf link; in untimed tests also late hard items did.
limits: Untimed comparison is a reanalysis of previous data, not a randomized comparison.
agent_relevance: Under speed WM predicts easy items; with time, other processes decide the hard items. Test an agent on easy and hard sets with and without extended thinking.

source: Colom et al. (2015) Fluid intelligence and working memory capacity: Is the time for working on intelligence problems relevant for explaining their large relationship? Pers Individ Differ 79, 75-80
finding: Failed replication of the monotone time effect: latent Gf-WMC correlation stayed high at every time limit and did not fall with more time.
numbers: N = 302 randomized to RAPM 20 (n=93), 30 (n=99) or 40 min (n=110). Latent r = .89 (20 min), .74 (30), .96 (40); weighted mean .86 (CI .83-.89). Not monotone.
limits: University students; six WM tasks; only RAPM timing varied (other Gf tests per manual); 40-min group is near the standard.
agent_relevance: The time moderator is contested. Do not build the agent around it without our own test.

source: Colom et al. (2015), score effects
finding: More time raised mean Raven scores substantially, yet the construct measured seemed unchanged. High-WM vs low-WM gap was smallest under the strictest time limit and grew with time.
numbers: d = .39 (20 vs 30 min), .58 (30 vs 40), 1.01 (20 vs 40). RAPM reliability .77, .76, .75. Raven correlation with the other two Gf tests similar across groups.
limits: Opposite to Chuderski prediction on the group-difference test.
agent_relevance: More time helps everyone and does not remove the WM gap, which argues against a pure compensation account.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick and Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer, Perspect Psychol Sci 11, 512-534
finding: Interventional test of capacity causality: training WM raises trained and near tasks but not Gf, which argues against capacity as a lever on intelligence.
numbers: 87 publications, 145 comparisons. Nonverbal ability g = 0.05 [-0.02, 0.13] (k=67, treated controls); 0.20 [0.11, 0.28] with untreated controls (k=53). Verbal WM near transfer g = 0.31; visuospatial 0.28; criterion tasks 0.80.
limits: Training may not raise capacity itself; mean group size about 22; follow-up (5 months) nonverbal g = -0.05.
agent_relevance: Cheap training-style shortcuts do not work. Gains are task-specific, so expect scaffold gains to be specific to what the scaffold supports.

source: Melby-Lervag et al. (2016), mediation and moderators
finding: Gains in WM did not predict gains in Gf; small studies and untreated controls inflate effects.
numbers: Nonverbal vs near-transfer WM gains beta = -.01, p=.86 (k=26). Studies with >=20 per group g = 0.01 (k=34) vs smaller 0.26 (k=25). N-back training g = 0.15, falling to 0.10 after removing one study.
limits: Mediation tests across studies have little power.
agent_relevance: Control condition choice matters more than the intervention: always compare to a treated control.

source: Melby-Lervag et al. (2016), publication bias
finding: P-curve shows no evidential value in treated-control studies, but evidential value in untreated-control studies.
numbers: Treated controls z(11) = -2.19, p=.01 (no evidential value); untreated z(16) = -3.41, p<.01.
limits: P-curve has limits with few studies.
agent_relevance: Positive reports of capacity training transfer are best explained by expectancy and control choice.

source: Dokic, Koso-Drljevic and Bilalic (2025) Past reflections, present insights: systematic review and new empirical research into the WMC-Gf relationship, Intelligence 108:101874
finding: Abstract page read: capacity hypothesis not supported in N = 543 by item difficulty, rule-token count, SEM or latent growth curve modelling. Systematic review found most studies did not show the predicted rise, a few did.
numbers: N = 543, non-Anglo-Saxon sample; operation, reading and symmetry span for WMC; Raven APM for Gf.
limits: Full text (PDF) returned HTTP 403; only the abstract page opened, so detailed coefficients not recorded here (see evidence_a for any numbers).
agent_relevance: Item difficulty and rule count must be measured per model, not assumed. Consistent with Frischkorn and Oberauer: a null is weakly informative too.

source: Dokic et al. (2025) read together with Frischkorn and Oberauer (2021)
finding: Interpretation: a null on the item-wise test does not refute capacity and a positive result would not prove it, because any pattern fits the hypothesis once sample mean capacity is allowed to vary.
numbers: Reasoning step, no new numbers. Compare: Little 2014 positive at N=126, Smolen 2015 inverted U at N=347 and 939, Dokic null at N=543.
limits: Frischkorn and Oberauer simulate; whether Dokic modelled sample mean capacity was not verified.
agent_relevance: Prefer experimental tests (vary load directly in a controlled item set) over correlational item curves.

source: Harrison, Shipstead and Engle (2015) Why is working memory capacity related to matrix reasoning tasks? Mem Cogn 43, 389-396
finding: Within-subjects replication of Wiley et al. (2011): novel-rule items did not correlate more with WMC than repeated-rule items. Seen only in search snippet this session.
numbers: Reported N = 99 in search summary (not verified in full text).
limits: Snippet only; not opened in this run (opened in evidence_a as a12).
agent_relevance: See a12 for full numbers. The new-rule account of difficulty fails to replicate.

source: Wiley, Jarosz, Cushen and Colflesh (2011) New rule use drives the relation between WMC and Raven APM, JEP:LMC 37, 256-263
finding: Claim that items needing a new rule combination correlate more with operation span; later not replicated (Harrison 2015; Smolen 2015). Abstract level only.
numbers: OSPAN-Raven r about .33 per Little et al.; token-wise r .25, .24, .33, .21.
limits: Search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Rule novelty may be a weak difficulty predictor.

source: Burgoyne and Engle (2020) Attention control: a cornerstone of higher-order cognition, Curr Dir Psychol Sci 29
finding: Rival to capacity: attention control explains shared variance of Gf, WM and even sensory discrimination. Gf-sensory link vanishes when attention control is added.
numbers: Tsukahara et al. (2020) N = 331: Gf-sensory discrimination direct path significant; with attention control as mediator the path became non-significant. Path labels in the figure (.79, .81, .74, .19) are read from garbled figure text, approximate.
limits: Review from the Engle lab; correlational mediation.
agent_relevance: Failures of an agent may come from distraction or goal loss rather than too few rule slots; add an attention/goal-maintenance check.

source: Burgoyne and Engle (2020), measurement problem
finding: Difference-score attention tasks (Stroop, flanker) are so unreliable that conclusions about attention control need latent variables.
numbers: With reasonable assumptions less than 10% of a difference score variance can reflect the construct.
limits: Statement of possibility, not an estimate for a specific task.
agent_relevance: Use composite scores across several items for any agent metric, not a single contrast.

source: Unsworth, Miller and Strayer (2024) Individual differences in attention control: a meta-analysis and re-analysis of latent variable studies, Psychon Bull Rev
finding: Attention-control factor found in most latent-variable studies and linked to Gf, WM and other abilities (abstract level).
numbers: 90 samples, over 23,000 participants; 84.4% found a coherent factor; mean loading .51 (per search summary).
limits: Search summary only; Gf coefficient not obtained.
agent_relevance: Supports giving the attention-control account weight beside capacity.

source: Kovacs and Conway (2016) Process overlap theory, Psychological Inquiry 27, 151-177
finding: Rival: positive manifold arises because tests draw on overlapping processes, so a single capacity need not cause Gf; abstract level only.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Implies difficulty comes from how many distinct processes an item overlaps, which supports measuring difficulty rather than counting rules.

source: REL: Evaluating Relational Reasoning in LLMs, arXiv 2604.12176 (v2 June 2026; authors not recorded)
finding: LLM version of the capacity test, using relational complexity (RC, number of jointly bound operands) rather than rule count. Accuracy falls with RC even when entity count is held fixed; entity count is a noisy difficulty proxy.
numbers: Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro Preview, GPT-5.2. Raven-type REL-A: RC=1 and 2 solved almost perfectly (91% on 30x30). On RC-scaling tasks Claude and Gemini fall to about 12% (chance 12.5%); GPT-5.2 drops about 40%. Headline: 45% drop from RC 3 to 9; 93% on the biology task.
limits: Synthetic generated tasks; 8-choice format; preprint.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that difficulty for LLMs follows binding arity, not rule or entity count. Measure RC in our items.

source: REL (arXiv 2604.12176), regression and mitigations
finding: On the biology task, RC explains the largest share of explainable variance, more than prompt length. The failure persists with more test-time compute and in-context examples.
numbers: Homoplastic-taxa count RC: accuracy 35% at 4 taxa to 1% at 25 taxa. RC explained 24% (Claude), 32% (Gemini), 44% (GPT) of explainable variance; next factor 7%, 17%, 6%. Raising the token cap changed accuracy about 0.4% on average.
limits: Three models; one task for the regression.
agent_relevance: Extra thinking tokens do not fix high-arity binding, so decomposition into lower-arity steps is the scaffold lever.

source: REL (arXiv 2604.12176), tensor tasks
finding: Counter-case: tensor tasks with high fixed RC improved with more input, since RC did not grow with size, showing size alone is not difficulty.
numbers: REL-A5 56-64% to 77-87% and REL-A6 41-50% to 53-64% on larger inputs; REL-A7 (RC=6) unsolved at any size.
limits: Same three models.
agent_relevance: Supports the correction in the subfield row: rule count or size alone is not the driver; the binding structure is.

source: Camposampiero, Hersche, Wattenhofer, Sebastian and Rahimi (2025) Can large reasoning models do analogical reasoning under perceptual uncertainty? arXiv 2503.11207
finding: o3-mini and DeepSeek R1 on I-RAVEN and I-RAVEN-X: longer rules and wider attribute ranges (more load) did little; perceptual uncertainty caused most of the loss.
numbers: o3-mini 86.6% on I-RAVEN to 17.0% (R1 80.6% to 23.2%) in the hardest uncertain setting. Longer rules/larger ranges alone cost o3-mini 5.6% and gave R1 a 2.2% gain. Chance 12.5%.
limits: Symbolic oracle input; two reasoning models; total drop up to 69.6% (o3-mini) and 57.2% (R1).
agent_relevance: A direct LLM analogue of Dokic: more rules and bigger matrices barely hurt, while noisy attributes do. Measure what actually hurts.
